name: Pennsylvania Dutch (Lehigh County)
family: Indo-European, Germanic, West Germanic, High German, Rhine Franconian (Palatine base)
variety: Eastern nonsectarian Pennsylvania Dutch (the speech of the Lutheran and Reformed 'church people') of Lehigh, Northampton and Berks counties, Pennsylvania, the variety on which the Buffington-Barba grammar and spelling are based
sources: Buffington, Albert F. and Barba, Preston A. (1954). A Pennsylvania German Grammar. Allentown: Schlechter's.
Frey, J. William (1942). A Simple Grammar of Pennsylvania Dutch. Clinton, South Carolina: Jacobs Press.
Reed, Carroll E. and Seifert, Lester W. (1954). A Linguistic Atlas of Pennsylvania German. Marburg.
Van Ness, Silke (1994). Pennsylvania German. In König and van der Auwera (eds.), The Germanic Languages. London: Routledge.
Louden, Mark L. (2016). Pennsylvania Dutch: The Story of an American Language. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
Kopp, Achim (1999). The Phonology of Pennsylvania German English as Evidence of Language Maintenance and Shift. Selinsgrove: Susquehanna University Press.
Keiser, Steven Hartman (2012). Pennsylvania German in the American Midwest. Publication of the American Dialect Society 96. Durham: Duke University Press.

Huffines, Marion Lois (1986). Intonation in language contact: Pennsylvania German English. In Enninger (ed.), Studies on the Languages and the Verbal Behavior of the Pennsylvania Germans I. Stuttgart: Steiner.
eSpeak NG voice and phoneme files for pdc-x-lehigh (espeak-ng-data/lang/gmw/pdc-x-lehigh, phsource/ph_pennsylvania_german_lehigh), whose comments state the dialect features the voice assumes.
contrasts: short versus long vowels, with a difference of quality: /ɪ/ versus /iː/, /ɛ/ versus /eː/, /ʊ/ versus /uː/, /ʌ/ versus /oː/, /ɑ/ versus /ɔː/
no front rounded vowels: the vowels of German schön, Tür, böse, Feuer are unrounded (schee, Dier, bees, Feier)
three diphthongs /aɪ aʊ ɔɪ/ (Deitsch, Haus, Boi)
long /æː/ (written ae: Kaes) versus /eː/ (written ee: schee)
back rounded long /ɔː/ (written aa: Baam, Fraa) versus /oː/ (written oo: Schprooch)
palatal and velar fricatives [ç x] and the weak voiced fricative [ɣ] between back vowels
lexical stress in prefixed words and loans
allophony: the lenis stops /b d ɡ/ are voiceless unaspirated lenes; the historical fortis /p t/ fell together with them in native words (Disch, Dochder, Babbier), while /k/ stays aspirated before a vowel and is lenis before a consonant (glee, Gnoche)
between vowels, historical /b/ is [v] (hawwe, gewwe) and historical /ɡ/ is [j] after front vowels, /r/ and /l/ and [ɣ] after back vowels (Reege, saage)
/r/ is a tongue-tip tap or short trill in all positions according to the voice files; use of the American English approximant is reported for some speakers of all groups
/r/ after a vowel is vocalised to [ɐ] or lost, giving centring diphthongs (Bier [biːɐ], Ohr [oːɐ]) and a final [ɐ] for -er
/l/ is clear in all positions according to the voice files; a dark /l/ after vowels is reported as English influence for speakers of all groups
front vowels keep their height before a vocalised /r/ ([eːɐ] in Baer, Kaer) according to the voice files
ch is palatal [ç] after front vowels and consonants and velar [x] after back vowels
s is voiceless in all positions and is [ʃ] before p and t
obstruents are voiceless at the end of a word
a vowel is inserted between /r/ or /l/ and a following velar or palatal consonant, and the spelling shows it (darich, Barig, Millich)
unstressed e is schwa; unstressed -er is [ɐ]
phonotactics: onset clusters with /ʃ/ before p, t, m, n, l, r, w and with /ɡ/ or /k/ before n and l; prefix vowel loss gives clusters such as gsch- and gf-
final unstressed -n of German is lost (wasche, schee)
short stressed vowels are followed by a consonant, which the spelling doubles

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the stem; the prefixes ge-, be-, ver- (fer-), er-, zer- are unstressed, separable particles and the first member of a compound are stressed, and loans keep the stress of the source word.
stress.cues: pitch movement, duration and intensity; unstressed syllables have schwa or [ɐ]

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed syllables mostly have [ə] or [ɐ]
rhythm.notes: No instrumental rhythm measurements are known to me.

length.notes: Vowel length is contrastive and tied to quality. Double consonant letters mark a short vowel; consonants are not long.

intonation.declarative: peaks on accented syllables, final fall to low
intonation.yes_no_question: rise to the last accented syllable followed by a fall on the syllables after it (a final rise-fall)
intonation.wh_question: accent on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise or high level at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: peak on the accented syllable followed by a fall
intonation.notes: The yes-no question pattern was described by Huffines for the English and the Pennsylvania Dutch of central and eastern Pennsylvania. The rest is low confidence.

problems: the stops b, d, g are inherited from the German table and are fully voiced; the descriptions have voiceless lenis stops
yes-no questions use tune q4, which ends in a rise; the documented pattern is a rise to the accented syllable followed by a final fall
stress is put on the first syllable of words that carry it later (Babbier is [ˈbɑbiːɐ])
English loans that keep their English spelling are read by the German-type letter rules; the pronunciation list has about 260 entries

the voice differs from the Lancaster voice in four settings only (au, r, l, and the vowel before vocalised r); other eastern features documented by Reed and Seifert, above all differences of vocabulary and word form, are not represented
the pronunciations have not been checked by native speakers (the voice is marked 'testing')
good: au is the diphthong [aʊ], r is a tap and l is clear, as the voice notes require
the unrounded vowel system, [ɔː] for aa, [æː] for ae and [ʌ] for short o follow the descriptions
vocalised r with centring diphthongs and [ɐ] for -er; intervocalic g is [j] or [ɣ]; final obstruents are devoiced

notes: Nonsectarian speakers are now mostly elderly, and the variety is receding (Louden 2016). The choice of tapped r and clear l for this voice follows the eSpeak NG voice files; the literature reports English-like r and dark l for some speakers of every group. No formant, duration or voice onset time values have been published that I can quote.
